milestones.title: an append-only run store keyed by config hash

functions.name: config_hash
functions.doc:
12 hex characters of the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of `config`.

Canonical means sorted keys and separators (",", ":"), so that
{"a": 1, "b": 2} and {"b": 2, "a": 1} hash alike.
>>> config_hash({"a": 1})
'015abd7f5cc5'

functions.name: RunStore.load
functions.doc:
Read self.path (if it exists) into self.records, keyed by "key".

A crash can leave half a line at the end, with no newline. Ignore
it, and cut it off the file, so that the next append is valid.

functions.name: RunStore.append
functions.doc:
Add one record: write dump_line(record) to the end of the file and
remember it in self.records. If its key is already there, raise
DuplicateKey and leave the file alone. Never rewrite old lines.

functions.name: RunStore.get
functions.doc: The record stored under `key`, or None.

functions.name: evaluate
functions.doc:
The run record for (config, seed). Train only if the store has no
record under run_key(config, seed); otherwise return the stored one.

A new record is a dict with exactly these fields:
kind "run", key, hash (config_hash), seed, config, proxy, heldout
(the two scores from train_and_score). Append it to the store.

milestones.checkpoint: check.py verifies: a hand-computed hash (the SHA-256 of {"a":1} starts 015abd7f5cc5); key order does not matter; the file holds exactly one dump_line per record; a duplicate key raises DuplicateKey and leaves the file alone; a reopened store has the same records; a torn last line is ignored and the next append still gives a valid file; evaluate trains once and then serves from the store, including after a reopen.
hints: json.dumps(config, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")), encoded to UTF-8, then hashlib.sha256(...).hexdigest()[:12].
To find the torn line, look at where the last newline is: text[:text.rfind("\n") + 1] is everything that was written completely.
Open for append with "a"; check the key before writing, so a refused record leaves no trace.
milestones.solution:
def config_hash(config):
    """12 hex characters of SHA-256 over the canonical JSON of config."""
    text = json.dumps(config, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
    return hashlib.sha256(text.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:12]

def run_key(config, seed):
    return f"{config_hash(config)}:{seed}"

class RunStore:
    """Append-only JSONL file. Opening an existing file loads it."""

    def __init__(self, path):
        self.path = path
        self.records = {}
        self.load()

    def load(self):
        """Read the file (if it exists) into self.records."""
        if os.path.exists(self.path):
            with open(self.path, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
                text = fh.read()
            keep = text[:text.rfind("\n") + 1]    # drop a torn last line
            if keep != text:
                with open(self.path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
                    fh.write(keep)
            for line in keep.splitlines():
                rec = json.loads(line)
                self.records[rec["key"]] = rec

    def append(self, record):
        key = record["key"]
        if key in self.records:
            raise DuplicateKey(key)
        with open(self.path, "a", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            fh.write(dump_line(record))
        self.records[key] = record

    def get(self, key):
        return self.records.get(key)

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.records)

def evaluate(config, seed, store):
    """The run record for (config, seed); train only if it is new."""
    key = run_key(config, seed)
    rec = store.get(key)
    if rec is None:
        proxy, held = train_and_score(config, seed)
        rec = {"kind": "run", "key": key, "hash": config_hash(config),
               "seed": seed, "config": config,
               "proxy": proxy, "heldout": held}
        store.append(rec)
    return rec
milestones.explain:
A research loop that cannot show its runs is a story. Autoresearch's own record is a results.tsv next to a git history: one line per experiment, with the commit, val_bpb, memory and a keep, discard or crash status (the format program.md asks the agent to write, in the version I read: commit 228791f of 25 March 2026). It is a good habit and a thin record. It holds the outcome of each comparison, not the runs behind it, and nothing stops a line being edited. The store you build here has three properties that the rest of the lab leans on.

Keyed by content. A run is identified by what was run: the config and the seed. Hash the config's canonical JSON (keys sorted, no spaces) with Secure Hash Algorithm 256 (SHA-256), a standard hash function, and keep 12 hex characters. The key is then hash:seed. Two configs that mean the same thing hash the same whatever order their keys were written in, and a config that differs in one digit hashes differently. This is the content-addressed cache of A0 chapter 22 and the same idea as a git commit id.

Append-only. Records are lines of JSON (the JSON Lines format, abbreviated JSONL), written one dump_line at a time to the end of the file, and a key that is already there is refused, not overwritten. The consequence is that the file is its own audit trail: to check a result you read it, and to claim a run happened you must have appended it. A crash can leave half a line at the end; your loader must drop that fragment instead of failing, and cut it off the file so the next append is valid.

A cache. evaluate(config, seed, store) trains only if the key is new. In the loop, the best config is compared with a fresh candidate on the same seeds again and again; the store makes every repeat free, and the count of real training runs becomes the loop's honest budget.
milestones.card:
A research loop is only believable if every run it did is written down once, never edited, and findable by what was run. So each run gets a key made from its settings and seed, runs are appended to a file that is never rewritten, and a repeated request is answered from the file, not by training again.

config_hash fingerprints the settings: two dictionaries that mean the same thing must hash alike, whatever order their keys were written in. run_key (given) joins that hash and the seed. append must refuse a stored key without touching the file. load must tolerate a torn last line: every complete line ends in a newline, so a fragment without one is the remains of a crash. evaluate trains only on a miss.

file: line h:1, line h:2, then {"key":"h:3","pr   (no newline)
load: keeps h:1 and h:2, cuts the file back to the end of h:2's line

Read more: A9 chapter 4, run tracking: a row that can be replayed.

milestones.title: a noise floor from baseline seeds

functions.name: mean
functions.doc: Arithmetic mean of a non-empty list.

functions.name: sample_sd
functions.doc:
Sample standard deviation: divide by n - 1, not n.
>>> round(sample_sd([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]), 4)
2.1381

functions.name: noise_floor
functions.doc:
Run `config` on every seed (through evaluate, so the store caches
them) and report how much it moves on its own. Returns

    {"n": len(seeds),
     "proxy":   {"mean": m, "sd": s, "floor": f},
     "heldout": {"mean": m, "sd": s, "floor": f}}

with floor = 1.96 * sqrt(2) * sd: the difference between two single
runs that reseeding alone produces 95% of the time.

milestones.task: Write mean, sample_sd and noise_floor(config, seeds, store). The last one runs every seed through evaluate (so the store caches them) and returns {"n", "proxy": {"mean", "sd", "floor"}, "heldout": {...}}.
milestones.checkpoint: check.py verifies: sample_sd([2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9]) is 2.1381 (not 2.0, which is the population value); a fake training function with proxy = seed gives mean 2.5, sd 1.2910 and floor 3.5785 on seeds 1 to 4; all runs land in the store; a second call trains nothing.
hints: If the standard deviation comes out as 1.118 instead of 1.291 for seeds 1 to 4, you divided by n.
Compute both scores in one loop over ("proxy", "heldout"); only the key into each record differs.
milestones.solution:
def mean(xs):
    return sum(xs) / len(xs)

def sample_sd(xs):
    """Standard deviation with n - 1 in the denominator."""
    m = mean(xs)
    return math.sqrt(sum((x - m) ** 2 for x in xs) / (len(xs) - 1))

def noise_floor(config, seeds, store):
    """How far two single runs of one config differ by reseeding alone."""
    recs = [evaluate(config, s, store) for s in seeds]
    out = {"n": len(recs)}
    for name in ("proxy", "heldout"):
        vals = [r[name] for r in recs]
        sd = sample_sd(vals)
        out[name] = {"mean": mean(vals), "sd": sd,
                     "floor": 1.96 * math.sqrt(2) * sd}
    return out
milestones.explain:
Run the baseline twice with different seeds and you get two different scores. Nothing changed except the random initial weights and the order of the minibatches, so the difference is the noise floor of the setup: the size of change that reseeding alone produces. Until you know it, "the score went from 0.333 to 0.318" is not a finding. Chapter 2 gives the theory and calls the standard deviation of the scores the noise floor; here you measure it, and the code also reports the larger number that governs a comparison of two single runs.

With K baseline runs, estimate the spread by the sample standard deviation s, which divides by K − 1 because the mean was estimated from the same data. A difference between two single runs has spread √2 times larger (the variances add), and 95% of such differences fall within 1.96 of those units. So the code's floor is:

floor = 1.96 × √2 × s

That is the size of gap that two runs of the same config exceed only one time in twenty. A single comparison that finds a candidate "better" by less than the floor has found nothing. The reference solution reports it for both scores, and the proxy's is four times the held-out one, which is the first thing this lab is built to show: a short run scored on a small slice is a noisy yardstick.
milestones.card:
Run the same setup twice with different random seeds and the scores differ, though nothing was changed. How large that difference gets by chance alone is the noise floor, and a gain smaller than it has shown nothing.

mean and sample_sd are the average and the standard deviation (the typical distance of a score from the mean), the latter dividing by n - 1 because the mean was estimated from the same scores. noise_floor(config, seeds, store) sends every seed through evaluate, so repeats come from the store, and reports mean, sd and floor for both scores a run gives, the cheap proxy and the held-out score. The floor is 1.96 * sqrt(2) * sd. The sqrt(2) is there because a difference of two noisy runs is noisier than one run (the variances add), and 1.96 covers 95% of such differences.

two seeds score 3 and 5: mean 4, sd 1.414, floor 3.92
a candidate that wins by 3 on single runs has shown nothing

Read more: A9 chapter 2, is 0.9170 better than 0.9210?

milestones.title: keep or revert on a paired test

functions.name: paired_test
functions.doc:
Test whether per-seed differences have a mean different from zero.

Returns (mean, sd, t, df, significant) where sd is the sample sd,
t = mean / (sd / sqrt(n)), df = n - 1 and significant means
abs(t) > t_critical(df). If sd == 0: t is 0.0 when the mean is 0,
else +inf or -inf by the sign of the mean.
>>> paired_test([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])      # (3.0, 1.5811, 4.2426, 4, True)

functions.name: keep_or_revert
functions.doc:
Decide whether `cand` replaces `best`, on the PROXY score only.

For each seed, run both configs on that same seed (through
evaluate) and take diff = best.proxy - cand.proxy (positive means
the candidate is better: scores are errors). Then paired_test.
Return {"keep": bool, "mean_gain": mean, "t": t, "df": df} where
keep is true only if the mean gain is positive AND significant.

milestones.task: Write paired_test(diffs), returning (mean, sd, t, df, significant), and keep_or_revert(best, cand, seeds, store), which runs both configs on every seed through evaluate, forms best.proxy - cand.proxy per seed and returns {"keep", "mean_gain", "t", "df"}. Decide on the proxy only.
milestones.checkpoint: check.py verifies: [1,2,3,4,5] gives mean 3, sd 1.5811, t = 4.243, significant; a mixed series with mean 0.1 is not; zero spread is handled (t = 0, or ±infinity for a nonzero mean); over 4,000 seeded no-effect trials the rule keeps about 2.5% while a single comparison keeps about half; a fake task with huge shared seed noise and a 0.10 gain is kept because the seeds are paired; a worse or identical candidate is reverted; a 0.05 gain buried in 0.4 of independent noise is almost never kept.
hints: With zero spread you would divide by zero. Return t = 0.0 when the mean is 0 as well, and math.copysign(math.inf, mean) otherwise.
The sign matters: a large negative t is a significant loss. Keep only if the mean gain is positive and the test is significant.
milestones.solution:
def paired_test(diffs):
    """(mean, sd, t, df, significant) for per-seed differences."""
    n = len(diffs)
    m = mean(diffs)
    sd = sample_sd(diffs)
    if sd == 0:
        t = 0.0 if m == 0 else math.copysign(math.inf, m)
    else:
        t = m / (sd / math.sqrt(n))
    df = n - 1
    return m, sd, t, df, abs(t) > t_critical(df)

def keep_or_revert(best, cand, seeds, store):
    """Keep `cand` only if it beats `best` on the proxy, paired by seed."""
    diffs = []
    for s in seeds:
        b = evaluate(best, s, store)["proxy"]
        c = evaluate(cand, s, store)["proxy"]
        diffs.append(b - c)           # positive: the candidate is better
    m, sd, t, df, sig = paired_test(diffs)
    return {"keep": m > 0 and sig, "mean_gain": m, "t": t, "df": df}
milestones.explain:
The rule in autoresearch's program.md is to keep a change if val_bpb is lower than before. With one run on each side, a change that does nothing at all beats a typical best score about half the time. After a lucky accept the bar is that lucky run, so later no-ops pass less often, but then the loop ratchets on luck instead of on effect. Over 100 overnight experiments the result is a stream of accepted changes that were not improvements, each built on top of the last. The fix is to ask a statistical question instead: is the mean difference over several seeds larger than the seed-to-seed variation of those differences?

Two choices make the test sharp. First, pair the runs: run the best config and the candidate on the same seeds, and look at the difference per seed, di = best − candidate (scores are errors, so a positive d means the candidate is better). Anything that moves both runs of a seed together, such as an unlucky initialisation, cancels in the difference, and what is left is the candidate's effect plus the noise that the two runs do not share. Second, test the mean of the differences with a paired t-test:

t = d̄ / (sd / √n)

where d̄ is the mean difference, sd their sample standard deviation and n the number of seeds. With n = 5 there are 4 degrees of freedom, and the two-sided 95% critical value of Student's t is 2.776, so the candidate is kept only if its mean gain is positive and |t| exceeds that. The lab gives you a table of critical values; the paired test itself is yours.

The test has a limit that milestone 3's own check does not hide. A paired test is very sensitive when the effect is consistent, and it will call a change "significant" even if it is tiny. The demo run at the end of this page keeps one experiment whose gain rounds to 0.0000 with t = 6.1, because a change to the L2 penalty shifted every seed by the same sliver. Significance says the effect is real; it does not say it is worth keeping. The noise floor of milestone 2 is the natural yardstick for "worth"; a minimum effect is one of the exercises under Going further.
milestones.card:
With no real difference between two versions, one run of each is a coin toss: either can come out lower. A paired test removes most of that luck: run both on the same seeds, take the difference per seed, and keep the change only if the average difference is clearly bigger than the wobble among those differences.

paired_test(diffs) turns the per-seed differences into t = mean / (sd / sqrt(n)), the average gain counted in units of its own uncertainty (sd is the sample standard deviation). It also returns df, the degrees of freedom (n - 1), and whether |t| beats t_critical(df) (given). keep_or_revert evaluates both configs on every seed and forms best.proxy - cand.proxy, the proxy being the cheap score the loop decides on; scores are errors, so positive means the candidate is better. Keep only if the mean is positive and significant, because the test also flags significant losses.

diffs 0.2, -0.1, 0.3, 0.0, 0.1: mean 0.1, sd 0.158, t = 1.41
df 4 needs |t| above 2.776, so this positive average is reverted

Read more: A9 chapter 2, paired tests over seeds.

milestones.title: proxy and held-out, logged for every experiment

functions.name: run_experiment
functions.signature: def run_experiment(index, best, cand, store, k=5):
functions.doc:
One experiment: decide on the proxy, log both scores.

seeds = experiment_seeds(index, k). Decide with keep_or_revert.
heldout_gain = mean over the same seeds of best.heldout - cand.heldout
(also through evaluate). The held-out score never affects "keep".
Append and return this record:

    kind "experiment", key f"exp:{index:04d}", index,
    best_hash (config_hash of best), cand_config, seeds, keep, t,
    proxy_gain (the decision's mean_gain), heldout_gain,
    gap (proxy_gain - heldout_gain)

functions.name: research_loop
functions.signature: def research_loop(proposer, n, store, k=5, start=None):
functions.doc:
Run n experiments. Start from a copy of `start` (default BASELINE).

For i in range(n): cand = proposer.propose(best, i), then
run_experiment(i, best, cand, store, k); if it was kept, the
candidate becomes the best. Return (best_config, list_of_records).

milestones.task: Write run_experiment(index, best, cand, store, k), which appends and returns the experiment record (kind "experiment", key "exp:0003" for index 3, and the fields above), and research_loop(proposer, n, store, k, start), which asks proposer.propose(best, i) for each candidate, keeps the winner as the new best and returns (best, history).
milestones.checkpoint: check.py verifies: a fake task where the proxy improves with the learning rate but the held-out score worsens is still kept (held-out never decides) and logs a negative held-out gain and the right gap; the proposer is shown the kept config and not the reverted one; every experiment is in the store with fresh seeds; on the real task, 12 experiments train every (config, seed) pair exactly once.
hints: The decision comes from keep_or_revert; call evaluate again for the held-out numbers, it is a cache hit.
Copy the start config with dict(start or BASELINE) so the module constant is never changed.
milestones.solution:
def run_experiment(index, best, cand, store, k=5):
    seeds = experiment_seeds(index, k)
    dec = keep_or_revert(best, cand, seeds, store)
    held = [evaluate(best, s, store)["heldout"]
            - evaluate(cand, s, store)["heldout"] for s in seeds]
    proxy_gain = dec["mean_gain"]
    held_gain = mean(held)
    rec = {"kind": "experiment", "key": f"exp:{index:04d}",
           "index": index, "best_hash": config_hash(best),
           "cand_config": cand, "seeds": seeds, "keep": dec["keep"],
           "t": dec["t"], "proxy_gain": proxy_gain,
           "heldout_gain": held_gain, "gap": proxy_gain - held_gain}
    store.append(rec)
    return rec

def research_loop(proposer, n, store, k=5, start=None):
    """n experiments; returns (best_config, list of experiment records)."""
    best = dict(start or BASELINE)
    history = []
    for i in range(n):
        cand = proposer.propose(best, i)
        rec = run_experiment(i, best, cand, store, k)
        history.append(rec)
        if rec["keep"]:
            best = cand
    return best, history
milestones.explain:
Now the extension that makes this Artifact 1 and not a re-implementation. The loop sees one number, the proxy, because it is cheap: in autoresearch it is the val_bpb after five minutes. What you want is a model that is better at the thing the proxy stands in for. The two can come apart, and the way to find out is to compute the second number for every experiment and write it next to the first. The held-out number must never be used in keep_or_revert; if it were, it would become part of what the loop optimises and stop being a check. This is the same discipline as the search, selection and test sets of A7 chapter 16.

An experiment now produces one record with: the experiment index, the hash of the best config, the candidate config, the seeds used, the decision, the proxy gain (the decision's mean gain), the held-out gain (the mean over the same seeds of best.heldout - cand.heldout) and their gap, proxy gain minus held-out gain. A positive gap on a kept experiment says the proxy flattered the change.

Two details are easy to get wrong. Fresh seeds per experiment: experiment_seeds(index, k) gives each experiment its own K seeds. If every experiment reused seeds 0 to 4, the loop would slowly select for configs that happen to suit those five initialisations, and the baseline would be measured on the same lucky draws every time. One training run per key: the best config appears in every experiment but on different seeds, so most of its runs are new, and your store must train each (config, seed) pair exactly once.
milestones.card:
A loop decides with a cheap number, the proxy, but what you care about is a slower number on data the loop never sees, the held-out score. Record both for every experiment but let only the proxy decide: if the held-out score decided, it would become one more thing the loop optimises and stop being a check.

run_experiment takes its seeds from experiment_seeds (given: fresh ones per experiment, so decisions do not share luck), decides with keep_or_revert, and reads the held-out scores through evaluate too. The held-out gain is best minus candidate, averaged over the same seeds; the gap is proxy gain minus held-out gain. research_loop works on a copy of start, never the module's BASELINE, and shows the proposer the best kept config, never a reverted one.

proxy gain +0.03, held-out gain -0.01: still kept (proxy decides)
gap = 0.03 - (-0.01) = +0.04, a change the proxy flattered

Read more: A9 chapter 2, the proxy and the thing you care about.

milestones.title: the gap, its trend, and a text chart

functions.name: cumulative
functions.doc:
Running totals over the history, one entry per experiment:
(cum_proxy, cum_heldout, cum_gap), where only KEPT experiments add
their proxy_gain and heldout_gain, and cum_gap = cum_proxy - cum_heldout.

functions.name: ols_slope
functions.doc:
Least-squares slope of ys against x = 0, 1, 2, ...
>>> ols_slope([1, 3, 5, 7])
2.0

functions.name: detect_overfit
functions.doc:
First index i (at least window - 1) at which, over the last
`window` experiments ending at i, BOTH hold:
  - the gap (cum_proxy - cum_heldout) has ols_slope >= min_slope, and
  - cum_heldout has ols_slope <= 0 (the held-out gain is not growing).
Return None if that never happens.

functions.name: text_chart
functions.doc:
Two bars per checkpoint, every `every` experiments.

scale = max(max(cum_proxy), max(cum_heldout), 1e-12)
For i in every-1, 2*every-1, ... and for ("P", cum_proxy[i]) then
("H", cum_heldout[i]): n = max(0, round(width * v / scale)) and the line
    f"{i + 1:>4} {tag} {'#' * n:<{width}} {v:+.4f}"
Return the lines joined by newlines (no trailing newline).

milestones.task: Write cumulative(history) (one entry per experiment; only kept experiments add), ols_slope(ys), detect_overfit(cum_proxy, cum_heldout, window, min_slope) (the first index where both conditions hold, or None) and text_chart(cum_proxy, cum_heldout, every, width) in exactly the format of its docstring.
milestones.checkpoint: check.py verifies: slopes of simple lines; a hand-built history; a detector that fires at the end of the first full window when the proxy climbs by 1 per step and the held-out is flat, stays silent when both climb together or when the held-out still climbs slowly, and stays silent with fewer experiments than one window; the chart against an exact expected string, and negative values; three complete 60-experiment loops in which the detector must fire and the proxy gain must dwarf the held-out gain.
hints: In cumulative, append the running totals for every experiment, kept or not; a reverted experiment repeats the previous value.
For the slice of a window ending at i, use [i - window + 1 : i + 1].
The chart line is f"{i + 1:>4} {tag} {'#' * n:<{width}} {v:+.4f}"; round, not int, for the bar length.
milestones.solution:
def cumulative(history):
    """Running totals over kept experiments: proxy, heldout and gap."""
    p = h = 0.0
    cp, ch, cg = [], [], []
    for rec in history:
        if rec["keep"]:
            p += rec["proxy_gain"]
            h += rec["heldout_gain"]
        cp.append(p)
        ch.append(h)
        cg.append(p - h)
    return cp, ch, cg

def ols_slope(ys):
    """Least-squares slope of ys against 0, 1, 2, ..."""
    n = len(ys)
    xbar = (n - 1) / 2
    ybar = mean(ys)
    num = sum((i - xbar) * (y - ybar) for i, y in enumerate(ys))
    den = sum((i - xbar) ** 2 for i in range(n))
    return num / den

def detect_overfit(cum_proxy, cum_heldout, window=10, min_slope=0.002):
    """First index where, over the last `window` experiments, the proxy
    gain climbs at >= min_slope per experiment while the held-out gain
    does not climb at all (its slope is <= 0)."""
    for i in range(window - 1, len(cum_proxy)):
        lo = i - window + 1
        gap = [p - h for p, h in zip(cum_proxy[lo:i + 1],
                                     cum_heldout[lo:i + 1])]
        if (ols_slope(gap) >= min_slope
                and ols_slope(cum_heldout[lo:i + 1]) <= 0):
            return i
    return None

def text_chart(cum_proxy, cum_heldout, every=10, width=30):
    scale = max(max(cum_proxy), max(cum_heldout), 1e-12)
    lines = []
    for i in range(every - 1, len(cum_proxy), every):
        for tag, v in (("P", cum_proxy[i]), ("H", cum_heldout[i])):
            n = max(0, round(width * v / scale))
            lines.append(f"{i + 1:>4} {tag} {'#' * n:<{width}} {v:+.4f}")
    return "\n".join(lines)
milestones.explain:
A single experiment's gap is mostly noise. What you want is the trend: does the proxy keep rising while the held-out score stops? Sum the gains of the kept experiments as they happen. The cumulative proxy gain is how far the loop thinks it has come; the cumulative held-out gain is how far it has really come; the cumulative gap is the difference. A slope of the gap over a recent window answers "is the loop still telling the truth?". The slope of a list of numbers against 0, 1, 2, ... is the least-squares line, which has a closed form: the sum of (x − mean x)(y − mean y) divided by the sum of (x − mean x)².

A rising gap on its own is not a fault. Early gains are often real on both scores, and a short run can gain more than a long one from the same change (a higher learning rate helps 40 steps more than 300). The detector therefore asks for two things in the same window: the gap slopes up by at least min_slope per experiment, and the cumulative held-out gain has stopped rising (slope at most zero). Proxy climbing while held-out is flat is what overfitting to the proxy looks like in a log. This is the 'sustained trend' of the artifact standards, applied in the opposite direction: a trend of the proxy that the held-out score does not share.

Last, a text chart, because a chart that needs a plotting library will not be in the log's directory when a reviewer opens it. Every every experiments, print two bars scaled to the largest cumulative value: P for the proxy and H for the held-out. A negative gain draws no bar, but its signed number stays on the line.
milestones.card:
One experiment's gap, proxy gain minus held-out gain, is mostly noise, but a trend is not. Add up the gains of the kept experiments as they happen: a proxy total (what the loop climbs) that keeps rising while the held-out total (what it cannot see) has stopped is a loop overfitting its own yardstick.

cumulative(history) returns three lists with one entry per experiment, so a reverted experiment repeats the previous total. ols_slope(ys) is the least-squares slope of ys against 0, 1, 2, ...: the sum of (x - mean x)(y - mean y) over the sum of (x - mean x) squared. detect_overfit slides a window along the totals and fires only when the gap is rising and the held-out total is not. A short run can gain more than a long one from a real change, so a widening gap alone proves nothing. text_chart follows its docstring exactly.

milestones.title: byte-identical replay from the log

functions.name: first_difference
functions.doc:
1-based number of the first line at which the two files differ
(compare bytes; a shorter file differs at its first missing line),
or None if they are byte-identical.

functions.name: replay
functions.doc:
Re-execute the log at `path` into a fresh store at out_path.

Delete out_path if it exists; make a RunStore there; best = a copy of
BASELINE. Then, for each record of `path`, in file order:
  "run"        -> evaluate(config, seed, store)
  "experiment" -> run_experiment(index, best, cand_config, store,
                                 len(seeds)); if kept, cand is the best
Return first_difference(path, out_path): None means byte-identical.

milestones.checkpoint: check.py verifies: the comparison on small files (equal, changed line, shorter, longer); for two seeds, a noise floor plus a 15-experiment loop written to a store is replayed into a new file and the bytes are identical; a score edited by 0.01 on one line of a copy is reported at exactly that line.
hints: Delete out_path first if it exists; a store appends, and an old file would hold stale records.
If the replay differs on line 1 of a log that you believe is clean, look for a record field that is not a function of the config and the seed.
milestones.solution:
def first_difference(path_a, path_b):
    """1-based number of the first differing line, or None if the two
    files are byte-identical."""
    with open(path_a, "rb") as fa, open(path_b, "rb") as fb:
        a = fa.read().split(b"\n")
        b = fb.read().split(b"\n")
    for i in range(max(len(a), len(b))):
        la = a[i] if i < len(a) else None
        lb = b[i] if i < len(b) else None
        if la != lb:
            return i + 1
    return None

def replay(path, out_path):
    """Re-execute every record of the log at `path` into a fresh store
    at out_path, in file order; then compare the two files."""
    if os.path.exists(out_path):
        os.remove(out_path)
    store = RunStore(out_path)
    best = dict(BASELINE)
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        for line in fh:
            rec = json.loads(line)
            if rec["kind"] == "run":
                evaluate(rec["config"], rec["seed"], store)
            else:
                again = run_experiment(rec["index"], best,
                                       rec["cand_config"], store,
                                       len(rec["seeds"]))
                if again["keep"]:
                    best = rec["cand_config"]
    return first_difference(path, out_path)
milestones.explain:
A log you cannot re-run is a claim. The test of whether your loop is a research instrument is whether someone else, holding only the log, can reproduce it: not "get similar numbers" but the same bytes. That is possible here because every record is a pure function of (config, seed) and the order of events, and the order is in the file. The one rule is that nothing else may enter a record: no timestamp, no hostname, no wall-clock duration, no process id. The moment a record holds the time it took, replay can never match, and you have to choose between a log with the timing in it and a log that proves itself. The usual answer is two files: a deterministic log for replay and a separate, disposable one for timing. Autoresearch's wall-clock budget is a version of the same problem, which Workbench 1 measures: a run that stops after thirty seconds does a different number of steps on a busy machine.

Write first_difference(path_a, path_b), which returns the 1-based number of the first line at which the two files differ as bytes (a shorter file differs at its first missing line), or None. Then replay(path, out_path): read the log in file order, re-execute each record into a brand-new store (a run record by calling evaluate; an experiment record by calling run_experiment with its logged candidate and the best so far), and return first_difference(path, out_path). If someone edited a score in the original, the re-executed value disagrees and the replay names the line.
milestones.card:
A log you cannot re-run is only a claim, so the test of a log is whether someone holding only the log can re-run it and get the same bytes, not merely similar numbers. That works only if each record depends on nothing but its config, its seed and the order of events: no clock, no machine name.

first_difference(path_a, path_b) compares two files as bytes and returns the 1-based number of the first line that differs, or None; a shorter file differs at its first missing line. replay(path, out_path) re-executes the log into a fresh store, in file order. A run record goes back through evaluate, and an experiment record through run_experiment with its logged candidate and seed count; a kept candidate becomes the best for the records after it. It returns the comparison of the original and the copy.

original A B C, replay A X C  ->  2   (line 2 differs)
original A B,   replay A B C  ->  3   (line 3 is missing)
